title: Early Life and Family History
description: The interview begins with introductions and Hazel Corbeill explaining the complex story of her parentage. Her biological father was killed before she was born, and her mother remarried a man named Weisenberg, whose name Hazel was given. She recounts the relief she felt upon learning the truth about her cruel stepfather just before her own wedding.

title: Arranged Marriage and Lost Education
description: Hazel describes being married at 16 to a man chosen by her family, a union that lasted 17 years despite their lack of common ground. She discusses the social norms of the time, including early marriages often being due to pregnancy, and laments that marriage ended her formal education, which she deeply loved.

title: Childhood, Hard Work, and Family Moves
description: Hazel details her difficult childhood, marked by constant moving and the necessity of hard work from a young age. She describes tasks like herding cows while crocheting lace for money and wearing ill-fitting shoes bought by her penny-pinching stepfather, which caused lifelong foot problems. Despite the hardships, she reflects on how these experiences built her understanding of others.

title: Journey West and Mother's Ingenuity
description: The conversation shifts to the family's two-month journey from Iowa to Idaho in a homemade car made from a Detroiter body on a Ford chassis. Hazel also talks about her mother, Lily Hong, a Norwegian immigrant and skilled seamstress who always found ways to earn money, including a detailed account of how she would card wool to make quilt bats.

title: Family Records and Later Life
description: Hazel provides specific dates and details about her parents, including her mother's birth and death and her biological father's family. She shares the story of her attempt as a young woman to connect with her paternal grandmother in Niagara Falls, which was ultimately unsuccessful due to family secrets.

title: Children's births; sons' names and occupations
description: Hazel Corbeill vividly describes her first childbirth in a boarding house outside Kellogg, where her mother-in-law refused to send for the doctor until roomers intervened. She then gives the names, birth dates, and current occupations of her sons Roy, Richard, and David, touching on Roy's forestry career, Richard's Air Force service, and David's teaching. She also mentions grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

title: Family generations; schooling and spelling bees
description: Corbeill and the interviewer compare families in which a niece or nephew is the same age as a child, and Corbeill describes rarely seeing her Air Force son's children while she ran her shop. She then tells of attending about 24 schools as an honor student, clashing with a Kellogg superintendent, and winning a Spokane radio spelling bee four weeks running after educating herself with a dictionary.

title: 1940 census; elections; hardware store
description: Corbeill recounts taking the 1940 census in the poorer parts of Kellogg and being named Idaho's outstanding enumerator by Congressman Compton I. White. She explains how her census friendships and her war-years hardware store work fed her runs for state representative and state senator, the first woman candidate in the county, and describes learning retail from her boss, known as Mother Hegbot.

title: Borrowing money and buying the flower shop
description: She tells how she borrowed $3,000 from an elderly couple who had been her customers and bought a rundown flower shop in 1943 even though she knew nothing of floristry. She contrasts her drive with the previous owners' advice to barely keep stock, and describes reinventing the business with gifts and artificial arrangements while living over the shop with her second husband and baby.

title: Second marriage; husband's decline and death
description: Corbeill describes her marriage to Vance Corbeill as very happy, praising his gentle nature, while noting his inability to run the shop and the bitter decline caused by hardening of the arteries, strokes, and rest home care. She gives his 1901 birth in Phoenix, B.C., the family's mining-town moves, their 1947 wedding in Kellogg, and his death the previous Thanksgiving.

title: Painting and dried flowers; design awards
description: Corbeill shows her oil paintings, begun in a recent art class, and dried-flower arrangements she sells from milkweed pods and rose hips. She describes teaching herself floral design, winning Inland Empire and Northwest competitions, and holding FTD offices as the first woman chairman, noting that only 10 of 91 national districts were represented by women.

title: Why she stayed in Kellogg
description: Asked why she stayed in the small town, she jokes that she just happened to get dumped there but had moved about 24 times as a child, so settling in Kellogg also meant finally putting down roots with her business.

title: Postwar strikes and declining a Spokane job; son's athletics; writing, sewing, and rest home requests
description: Hazel Corbeill describes the yearly strikes after World War II and the strain on her flower shop. She turned down well-paid design work in Spokane because of her husband Vance's roots and her son's baseball and YMCA activities. After retirement she considered moving to Coeur d'Alene, has published articles in the FTD trade journal, and avoids sewing requests from rest home residents tied to her childhood chores. Connie Richard closes the interview.
